Measurement of PSA is the cornerstone of follow-up after local treatment. While PSA thresholds depend on the
local treatment used, PSA recurrence almost always precedes clinical recurrence [1436, 1437]. The key question
is to establish when a PSA rise is clinically significant since not all PSA increases have the same clinical value

interventions.body:
WHAT I FOUND
**radiology_report**: The MRI prostate exam showed a focal hypo-intense lesion in the peripheral zone at the base/mid right, measuring approximately 12 mm. On DWI, the lesion showed restricted diffusion with high signal on b=1400 and corresponding low ADC values. Dynamic contrast-enhanced sequences revealed early, intense enhancement. Impression was PI-RADS v2.1: 5 (highly suspicious for clinically significant prostate cancer). Clinical T stage was cT2a.
**pathology_report**: Biopsy 1 (May 2024) and Biopsy 2 (December 2024) both revealed adenocarcinoma of the prostate, Gleason score 3+3, ISUP grade group 1, with perineural invasion present. The histological findings remained stable across both timepoints, showing persistent low-grade disease with perineural invasion. AI-predicted ISUP grade group (digital pathology) was grade group 2.
**previous_notes**: Notes from May 2024 indicated a PSA of 3.5 ng/mL, DRE was unremarkable, MRI showed PI-RADS 4 lesion, and a systematic biopsy revealed Gleason 3+3 ISUP GG1. The patient opted for surveillance with 6-monthly PSA monitoring and repeat MRI in 12 months.
**family_history**: Not recorded.
**psa_trend**: The PSA trend shows values of 3.3 ng/mL in July 2023, 2.2 ng/mL in November 2023, 2.2 ng/mL in April 2024, 3.5 ng/mL in August 2024, and 7.6 ng/mL in January 2025.
**laboratory_results**: The most recent PSA was 7.6 ng/mL on November 26, 2024. Free PSA was 0.93 ng/mL (12%), and other routine labs (Haemoglobin, WBC, Platelets, Creatinine, eGFR, Testosterone, Alkaline phosphatase, LDH) were within normal or acceptable ranges.

WHAT IS NOT RECORDED
Family history information is not recorded.

WHAT THIS SUPPORTS
The retrieved data strongly supports the need for a definitive management decision. The patient has a high-risk profile characterized by a rapidly rising PSA (from 3.3 to 7.6 ng/mL), a PI-RADS 5 lesion on MRI, and a confirmed Gleason 3+3 diagnosis with perineural invasion from two separate biopsies. The pathology confirms persistent low-grade disease. The guidelines suggest MRI-directed biopsy is the standard, and the current data necessitates a review of the active surveillance protocol given the high PSA and high-risk imaging findings.
